hook: Llama 3 and Qwen 3 are GPT-2 with four swaps. Make those swaps and real Qwen3 weights load into your own code.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Llama 3 and Qwen 3 are GPT-2 with four swaps. Make those swaps and real Qwen3 weights load into your own code.

0:15 QUESTION — Every open frontier-ish model since 2023 shares one skeleton. If you can diff it against the GPT you built in module 5, you can read any new model card in five minutes. The proof is loading Qwen3-0.6B into your class and getting identical logits.

1:00 INTUITION — Think of GPT-2 as a car and Llama 3 as the same chassis with a new engine, suspension and steering. RoPE instead of learned positions. RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm. SwiGLU instead of GELU MLP. Grouped-query attention instead of full multi-head. Qwen3 adds one more part: QK-norm. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — RMSNorm: y = x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * g, no mean subtraction, no bias. SwiGLU: FFN(x) = W_down( silu(W_gate x) * (W_up x) ). RoPE: rotate each pair of q and k dims by angle m * theta_i, theta_i = base^(-2i/d); Llama 3 uses base 500000, Qwen3 uses 1000000. GQA: H_q query heads share H_kv key-value heads, groups = H_q / H_kv. QK-norm: RMSNorm applied per head to q and k before RoPE. Config diff table on screen: GPT-2 small (12 layers, 768, 12 heads, 50257 vocab) vs Llama 3 8B (32 layers, 4096, 32 q heads, 8 kv heads, head_dim 128, FFN 14336, vocab 128256) vs Qwen3-0.6B (28 layers, 1024 hidden, 16 q heads, 8 kv heads, head_dim 128, FFN 3072, vocab 151936, tied embeddings).

4:30 CODE — Extend your GPTConfig with norm='rms', mlp='swiglu', pos='rope', n_kv_head, head_dim, qk_norm, rope_theta, tie_embeddings. Note Qwen3's head_dim times heads (2048) is not hidden size (1024), so q_proj is 1024 to 2048. Write load_qwen3(path) that reads model.safetensors with safetensors.torch.load_file and maps names: model.layers.{i}.self_attn.q_proj.weight to blocks[i].attn.wq.weight, q_norm, k_norm, mlp.gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj, input_layernorm, post_attention_layernorm. Use the half-split rotate_half RoPE convention that the HF checkpoint expects.

8:00 RECEIPT — Tokenize 'The capital of France is' with the Qwen3 tokenizer, run both your model and the HF reference (AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained('Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B', torch_dtype=torch.float32)), and torch.testing.assert_close(my_logits, hf_logits, atol=1e-4, rtol=1e-4). Greedy-generate 20 tokens from both; the token ids must be identical.

10:00 MEASURE — Parameter count per component for Qwen3-0.6B from your code: embeddings, attention, MLP, norms, and check the total against the model card (about 0.6B with tied embeddings, 0.44B non-embedding). Show how much of the model is embeddings at this size.

11:15 TAKEAWAY — Modern decoder LLMs are GPT-2 plus RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU and GQA, and Qwen3 adds QK-norm. Interview line: I can load a production checkpoint into my own implementation and match logits to 1e-4, which proves I understand every op.

interview_q: What changed between GPT-2 and Llama 3? Learned absolute positions became RoPE, LayerNorm became RMSNorm with pre-norm, the GELU MLP became SwiGLU, and multi-head attention became grouped-query attention to shrink the KV cache; newer models like Qwen3 also add QK-norm for stability.
explainer: Here is the GPT two block we built in module five. Embeddings, attention, MLP, two LayerNorms.
Swap one: learned position embeddings disappear. Instead, queries and keys get rotated by an angle that depends on position. That is RoPE.
Swap two: LayerNorm becomes RMSNorm. No mean subtraction, no bias, just divide by the root mean square.
Swap three: the MLP becomes SwiGLU. Two parallel projections, one gated by SiLU, multiplied together.
Swap four: thirty two query heads now share eight key value heads. That is grouped query attention.
Qwen three adds a small norm on each head's queries and keys before the rotation. That is QK norm.
Now the real Qwen three checkpoint flows into our class, tensor by tensor, by name.
Same prompt into both models. The two logit vectors overlap exactly. Our code is the model.

hook: A model trained on 2k tokens falls apart at 4k. Change one formula for the rotation frequencies and it keeps working, with no training.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — A model trained on 2k tokens falls apart at 4k. Change one formula for the rotation frequencies and it keeps working, with no training.

0:15 QUESTION — Qwen3 ships with a 32k context and recommends YaRN to reach 128k. DeepSeek-V3 used YaRN to go to 128k. How do you stretch RoPE without breaking what the model learned? We compare position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN on a real model.

1:00 INTUITION — RoPE is a set of clock hands spinning at different speeds. Fast hands encode fine local order, slow hands encode long range. Past the trained length, the slow hands land at angles the model never saw. Position interpolation slows every hand, which blurs local detail. YaRN slows only the slow hands and leaves the fast ones alone. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — RoPE frequencies theta_d = b^(-2d/|D|), wavelength lambda_d = 2 pi / theta_d. Scale factor s = L_new / L_train. Position interpolation: theta_d' = theta_d / s for all d. NTK-aware: change the base, b' = b * s^(|D|/(|D|-2)), which barely touches high frequencies and stretches low ones. YaRN, NTK-by-parts: ratio r_d = L_train / lambda_d, how many full turns dimension d makes in the training window. Ramp gamma(r) = 0 if r < alpha, 1 if r > beta, else (r - alpha)/(beta - alpha), with alpha = 1, beta = 32 for Llama. New frequency theta_d' = (1 - gamma) theta_d / s + gamma theta_d. Plus attention temperature: scale logits by 1/t with sqrt(1/t) = 0.1 ln(s) + 1, implemented by multiplying cos and sin by that factor so q dot k picks up its square.

6:00 CODE — def rope_inv_freq(dim, base) -> (dim/2,). def pi_inv_freq(..., s). def ntk_inv_freq(..., s). def yarn_inv_freq(dim, base, s, L_train, alpha=1, beta=32) -> (inv_freq, mscale). Patch the model's rotary module from last episode to accept a precomputed inv_freq and mscale. Experiment script: TinyLlama-1.1B (trained at 2048) on long documents, perplexity with sliding evaluation at 2k, 4k, 8k for none, PI, NTK, YaRN at s = 4, no fine-tuning. Use the MPS device and SDPA so 8k fits.

9:00 RECEIPT — Compare your yarn_inv_freq and mscale against Hugging Face transformers' YaRN init (transformers.modeling_rope_utils.ROPE_INIT_FUNCTIONS['yarn'] with a config whose rope_scaling is {'rope_type':'yarn','factor':4.0,'original_max_position_embeddings':2048}): torch.testing.assert_close on inv_freq and an exact match on the attention factor 0.1*ln(4)+1 = 1.1386. Then the published claim: YaRN without fine-tuning should hold perplexity near the 2k baseline past the training length while plain RoPE explodes.

11:00 MEASURE — Perplexity vs context length plot, four lines. Plain RoPE shoots up right after 2048. PI degrades the short-context perplexity a little. YaRN stays closest to baseline. Second plot: per-dimension scale factor theta_d'/theta_d for PI, NTK, YaRN.

12:15 TAKEAWAY — Extend context by stretching only the low-frequency RoPE dimensions and adding a small temperature. Interview line: YaRN interpolates dimensions whose wavelength exceeds the training length, extrapolates the high-frequency ones, and rescales attention logits by 0.1 ln s plus 1 squared.
13:00 NEXT — Next: KV cache math: MHA vs GQA vs MLA.
key_math: theta_d = b^{-2d/|D|}, r_d = L / lambda_d; gamma(r) = clamp((r - alpha)/(beta - alpha), 0, 1); theta_d' = (1-gamma) theta_d / s + gamma theta_d; sqrt(1/t) = 0.1 ln s + 1; NTK: b' = b s^{|D|/(|D|-2)}
code_task: rope_inv_freq, pi_inv_freq, ntk_inv_freq, yarn_inv_freq(dim, base, s, L_train, alpha=1, beta=32) -> (inv_freq (dim/2,), mscale); patched rotary embedding; perplexity sweep on TinyLlama-1.1B at 2k/4k/8k for each method.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(yarn_inv_freq(64, 10000, 4.0, 2048)[0], hf_inv_freq) against transformers' ROPE_INIT_FUNCTIONS['yarn'], attention factor == 0.1*math.log(4)+1; YaRN perplexity at 8k within a small margin of the 2k baseline while unscaled RoPE diverges.
gotchas: Applying the YaRN temperature to the logits and also to cos/sin, which squares it twice; mixing up wavelength and frequency in the ramp so the wrong dimensions get interpolated; recomputing RoPE caches at the old max length so positions past 2048 index out of range or wrap.
interview_q: How does YaRN extend a model's context window? It keeps high-frequency RoPE dimensions unchanged, interpolates low-frequency dimensions whose wavelength exceeds the training length by the scale factor, ramps between them, and adds a logit temperature, so local position resolution is preserved while long positions stay in-distribution.
explainer: Here is RoPE as a row of clock hands, each spinning at its own speed as position increases.
The fast hands make many turns inside the training window. The slow hands never complete even one turn.
Go past the training length and the slow hands land at angles the model has never seen. Perplexity explodes.
Position interpolation slows every hand by the same factor. Long positions are now familiar, but local detail gets squeezed.
NTK aware scaling changes the base instead, so the fast hands barely move and the slow ones stretch.
YaRN makes it explicit. Count turns per dimension. Many turns, leave it alone. Under one turn, interpolate. Ramp in between.
Longer contexts also flatten the attention pattern, so YaRN sharpens the softmax again with a small temperature factor.
On the plot, plain RoPE shoots up past two thousand tokens while YaRN stays flat to eight thousand.

hook: Llama 3 70B needs 320 kilobytes of KV cache for every token. DeepSeek-V3 is far bigger and needs about 69. Here is the math.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Llama 3 70B needs 320 kilobytes of KV cache for every token. DeepSeek V3 is far bigger and needs about 69. Here is the math.

0:15 QUESTION — At long context and large batch, the KV cache, not the weights, decides how many users fit on a GPU. That is why GQA and MLA exist. We build a calculator that reads real configs and check it against the bytes PyTorch actually allocates.

1:00 INTUITION — Every token you generate leaves a sticky note at every layer: its keys and values, so future tokens can look back. MHA writes a note per head. GQA shares notes across groups of heads. MLA writes one compressed note per layer and lets each head decode it. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Bytes per token = 2 (K and V) * n_layers * n_kv_heads * d_head * bytes_per_elem. MHA: n_kv_heads = n_heads. GQA: n_kv_heads = n_groups. MQA: 1. MLA caches the latent c_KV of size d_c plus the shared RoPE key of size d_h^R per layer, no factor 2: (d_c + d_h^R) * n_layers * bytes. Worked numbers in bf16: Llama 3 8B: 2*32*8*128*2 = 131,072 B = 128 KiB. Llama 3 70B: 2*80*8*128*2 = 320 KiB. Qwen3-0.6B: 2*28*8*128*2 = 112 KiB. DeepSeek-V3: (512+64)*61*2 = 70,272 B, about 69 KiB. DeepSeek-V2 says MLA's cache equals GQA with only 2.25 groups, since 576 / (2*128) = 2.25. Total cache = bytes_per_token * seq_len * batch.

5:00 CODE — def kv_bytes_per_token(cfg: dict, dtype_bytes=2) that branches on attention type: reads num_hidden_layers, num_key_value_heads, head_dim (or hidden_size/num_attention_heads), and for MLA kv_lora_rank and qk_rope_head_dim. Load real config.json files for Llama-3-8B, Llama-3-70B, Qwen3-0.6B, Mistral-7B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, DeepSeek-V3. def max_batch(cfg, gpu_bytes, weight_bytes, seq_len) for an 80 GB H100. Print a table.

8:00 RECEIPT — Run Qwen3-0.6B generation for 1000 tokens with Hugging Face's cache, then sum k.nbytes + v.nbytes over every layer of the returned past_key_values and assert it equals kv_bytes_per_token(qwen3_cfg) * 1000 * batch exactly. Then check DeepSeek-V3's ratio: MLA 576 elements per layer vs an MHA equivalent of 2*128*128 = 32,768, so 57x smaller per layer, and confirm the DeepSeek-V2 paper's '2.25 groups' equivalence.

10:00 MEASURE — Bar chart, log scale: KiB per token for each model. Second chart: max concurrent 32k-token sequences on one 80 GB H100 after weights, for Llama 3 8B MHA-hypothetical vs GQA vs an MLA-style variant.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — KV bytes per token is 2 times layers times KV heads times head dim times bytes, and MLA replaces that with latent plus RoPE dims. Interview line: GQA and MLA exist because decode is memory-bound and the KV cache caps batch size, so shrinking it buys throughput directly.
12:15 NEXT — Next: Multi-head latent attention, derived.
key_math: bytes/token = 2 * L * H_kv * d_h * b; MLA bytes/token = (d_c + d_h^R) * L * b; DeepSeek-V3: (512+64)*61*2 = 70,272 B; MLA = GQA with (d_c + d_h^R)/(2 d_h) = 2.25 groups
code_task: kv_bytes_per_token(cfg, dtype_bytes=2) handling MHA, GQA, MQA, MLA from HF config.json fields; max_batch(cfg, gpu_bytes, weight_bytes, seq_len); table and charts over six real configs.
receipt: sum(k.nbytes + v.nbytes for each layer of Qwen3-0.6B's past_key_values after 1000 tokens) == kv_bytes_per_token(cfg) * 1000 * batch; DeepSeek-V3 per-layer ratio 32768/576 and the 2.25-group equivalence from the DeepSeek-V2 paper.
gotchas: Using hidden_size / num_attention_heads as head_dim when the config sets head_dim explicitly (Qwen3: 128, not 64); forgetting that MLA has no separate K and V factor of 2 because one latent serves both; counting the HF cache before generation finishes or with a sliding-window cache that caps length.
interview_q: How big is the KV cache for Llama 3 70B at 32k context, batch 8, in bf16? 2 * 80 layers * 8 KV heads * 128 * 2 bytes = 320 KiB per token, times 32,768 tokens times 8 sequences is about 80 GiB, which is a full H100 just for cache.
explainer: Here is one token passing through a stack of layers. At every layer it leaves behind a key and a value.
With full multi head attention, that is a key and a value for every head. Thirty two pairs per layer.
Grouped query attention lets four query heads share one pair. The pile of notes shrinks by four.
Multi query goes all the way to one pair per layer. Small, but quality suffers.
Multi head latent attention stores one short compressed vector per layer, plus a tiny shared position key.
Stack it up across layers and tokens. Llama three seventy B is a tall tower. DeepSeek V three is short.
Divide what is left of an eighty gigabyte GPU by that tower, and you get how many users fit.
So the KV cache, not the weights, is what limits batch size at long context.

hook: DeepSeek caches one 512-number vector per token per layer and rebuilds 128 heads of keys and values from it on the fly.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — DeepSeek caches one 512 number vector per token per layer and rebuilds 128 heads of keys and values from it on the fly.

0:15 QUESTION — GQA shrinks the cache by sharing heads, and loses some quality. DeepSeek-V2 found a way to shrink it further and match or beat MHA: multi-head latent attention. We derive it from the paper's equations and build the forward pass.

1:00 INTUITION — Instead of storing every head's keys and values, store a short summary of the token and give each head its own decoder that expands the summary into that head's key and value. Low-rank compression, like storing a JPEG and decompressing on read. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — DeepSeek-V2 notation, h_t in R^d. KV down-projection: c_t^KV = W^DKV h_t, size d_c (512), much smaller than n_h d_h (128*128 = 16384). Up-projections per head: k_t^C = W^UK c_t^KV, v_t^C = W^UV c_t^KV. Queries are compressed too, to cut activation memory in training: c_t^Q = W^DQ h_t (d_c' = 1536), q_t^C = W^UQ c_t^Q. The position part, decoupled RoPE: q_t^R = RoPE(W^QR c_t^Q), one per head of size d_h^R = 64; k_t^R = RoPE(W^KR h_t), a single key shared by all heads. Per head: q_{t,i} = [q^C_{t,i}; q^R_{t,i}], k_{t,i} = [k^C_{t,i}; k^R_t]. o_{t,i} = sum_j softmax_j( q_{t,i}^T k_{j,i} / sqrt(d_h + d_h^R) ) v^C_{j,i}. u_t = W^O [o_{t,1}; ...; o_{t,n_h}]. Cached per token: c_t^KV and k_t^R, 576 numbers. Parameter view: W^UK W^DKV is a rank-512 factorization of a 16384 by 5120 key projection. DeepSeek-V3 adds RMSNorm on c^Q and c^KV.

6:00 CODE — class MLA(nn.Module) with args dim, n_heads, q_lora_rank, kv_lora_rank, qk_nope_head_dim, qk_rope_head_dim, v_head_dim. Layers: wq_a (dim -> q_lora_rank), q_norm, wq_b (q_lora_rank -> n_heads*(nope+rope)), wkv_a (dim -> kv_lora_rank + rope), kv_norm, wkv_b (kv_lora_rank -> n_heads*(nope+v)), wo (n_heads*v -> dim). Forward on x (B,T,dim): split wkv_a output into c_kv (B,T,512) and k_pe (B,T,64); apply RoPE to k_pe and q_pe; expand c_kv through wkv_b into k_nope (B,T,H,128) and v (B,T,H,128); k = cat(k_nope, k_pe.expand over heads); scores via SDPA with scale (nope+rope)**-0.5. Return out and the cache tuple (c_kv, k_pe). This is the naive, decompress-everything mode.

9:30 RECEIPT — Instantiate Hugging Face transformers' DeepSeek-V3 attention module with a tiny config (hidden 256, 4 heads, q_lora_rank 64, kv_lora_rank 32, nope 32, rope 16, v 32, rope_interleave matching yours), copy its weights into your MLA by name, and torch.testing.assert_close(my_mla(x)[0], hf_attn(x, ...)[0], atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-5) in float32. Also assert the cache per token is kv_lora_rank + qk_rope_head_dim numbers.

11:30 MEASURE — With DeepSeek-V2's real dims, print the parameter count of the attention block vs an MHA block of the same width, and the cache per token: MHA 32,768 vs MLA 576 elements per layer. Mention the paper's reported 93.3 percent KV cache reduction vs DeepSeek 67B.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — MLA caches a low-rank latent plus a small shared RoPE key and reconstructs per-head keys and values with up-projections. Interview line: MLA is low-rank joint compression of K and V; it cuts the cache like MQA while keeping per-head expressiveness through learned up-projections.
13:15 NEXT — Next: MLA weight absorption and decoupled RoPE.
key_math: c^KV = W^DKV h (d_c=512); k^C = W^UK c^KV, v^C = W^UV c^KV; c^Q = W^DQ h, q^C = W^UQ c^Q; q^R = RoPE(W^QR c^Q), k^R = RoPE(W^KR h) shared; score = [q^C;q^R]^T[k^C;k^R] / sqrt(d_h + d_h^R)
code_task: class MLA(nn.Module) with wq_a, q_norm, wq_b, wkv_a, kv_norm, wkv_b, wo; forward(x (B,T,dim), freqs) -> (out (B,T,dim), cache (c_kv (B,T,d_c), k_pe (B,T,d_rope))); naive decompress-then-attend mode.
receipt: Copy weights from transformers' DeepSeek-V3 attention module with a tiny random config and torch.testing.assert_close(my_mla(x)[0], hf_out, atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-5) in float32; cache size per token == kv_lora_rank + qk_rope_head_dim.
gotchas: Scaling scores by 1/sqrt(nope) instead of 1/sqrt(nope + rope); applying RoPE to the whole key instead of only the decoupled k_pe slice; DeepSeek checkpoints use the interleaved RoPE pair layout for the rope dims, so a half-split rotate_half gives close but wrong outputs.
interview_q: How does MLA reduce the KV cache without reducing the number of heads? It projects each token to a small shared latent c^KV and caches only that plus one small RoPE key; per-head keys and values are reconstructed with learned up-projection matrices, so all 128 heads keep distinct K and V.
explainer: Here is one token's hidden vector, about five thousand numbers wide, entering the attention layer of DeepSeek V two.
Normally it projects to keys and values for all one hundred twenty eight heads. Sixteen thousand numbers each.
MLA first squeezes the token down to a latent of just five hundred twelve numbers. This is what gets cached.
When attention runs, each head has its own up projection that expands the latent into that head's key and value.
Position needs special care, so a separate small key of sixty four numbers carries RoPE, shared by every head.
Each head's final key is its own decompressed content part glued to that one shared position part.
Queries are compressed and expanded the same way, which does not shrink the cache but saves activation memory in training.
The cache per token per layer drops from thirty two thousand numbers to five hundred seventy six.

hook: RoPE almost killed MLA. The rotation sits between two matrices you want to multiply together ahead of time. DeepSeek's fix is a side channel.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — RoPE almost killed MLA. The rotation sits between two matrices you want to multiply together ahead of time. DeepSeek's fix is a side channel.

0:15 QUESTION — Last episode we decompressed the latent into full keys and values every step. That throws away the decode speedup. The trick DeepSeek uses in its own inference code is weight absorption: never decompress. We derive it, show why RoPE breaks it, and prove the absorbed version is exactly equal.

1:00 INTUITION — If key equals W times latent, then query dot key equals (W transpose query) dot latent. So move W onto the query side once, and attend directly against the cached latents. It is associativity of matrix multiply, used as an inference optimization. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Content score for head i: (q^C_i)^T k^C_{j,i} = (q^C_i)^T W^UK_i c_j = (W^UK_i^T q^C_i)^T c_j. Define q~_i = W^UK_i^T q^C_i, size d_c. Score is q~_i dot c_j, no per-token key reconstruction. Value side: o_i = sum_j p_ij W^UV_i c_j = W^UV_i (sum_j p_ij c_j). So attention is computed over the latents and W^UV_i is applied once after, or folded into W^O. Effectively MQA with key dim d_c + d_h^R = 576 and value dim d_c = 512 shared by all heads. Why RoPE breaks it: with RoPE on the content key, score = (q^C_i)^T R_{t}^T R_{j} W^UK_i c_j = (q^C_i)^T R_{j-t} W^UK_i c_j. R_{j-t} depends on both positions, so W^UQ^T R W^UK cannot be precomputed. Decoupled fix: no RoPE on the compressed part; add separate q^R_i and a shared k^R_j that carry RoPE; total score = q~_i dot c_j + q^R_i dot k^R_j.

6:00 CODE — Add mode='absorb' to MLA. Reshape wkv_b weight to (H, nope+v, d_c), split into w_uk (H, nope, d_c) and w_uv (H, v, d_c). q_nope (B,T,H,nope) -> q_lat = einsum('bthd,hdc->bthc', q_nope, w_uk). scores = (einsum('bthc,bsc->bhts', q_lat, c_kv) + einsum('bthr,bsr->bhts', q_pe, k_pe)) * scale, causal mask, softmax. o_lat = einsum('bhts,bsc->bthc', p, c_kv); o = einsum('bthc,hvc->bthv', o_lat, w_uv); out = wo(o.flatten(2)). Decode step uses only the cache (c_kv, k_pe).

9:00 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(mla(x, mode='absorb'), mla(x, mode='naive'), atol=1e-10, rtol=1e-10) in float64, then 1e-5 in float32, with causal masking and a 1-token decode against a 1000-token cache. Cross-check with DeepSeek's reference inference code (deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3, inference/model.py), which ships both attn_impl 'naive' and 'absorb'. Negative control: put RoPE on the compressed key and show absorbed and naive no longer match.

11:00 MEASURE — Per-decode-step FLOPs and bytes read per layer at T_cache = 32k with V3 dims: naive (reconstruct K and V for every cached token, 128 heads) vs absorbed (read 576 numbers per cached token). Time both on the Mac with T_cache in {1k, 8k, 32k}.

12:15 TAKEAWAY — Absorb W^UK into the query and W^UV into the output so attention runs directly on cached latents; decoupled RoPE keeps that possible. Interview line: RoPE inserts a position-dependent rotation between W^UQ and W^UK, so DeepSeek routes positional information through separate small RoPE dims with a shared key.
13:00 NEXT — Next: Mixture of Experts: routing.
key_math: (q^C_i)^T W^UK_i c_j = (W^UK_i^T q^C_i)^T c_j; o_i = W^UV_i sum_j p_ij c_j; with RoPE: q^T R_{j-t} W^UK c_j (not precomputable); score = q~_i . c_j + q^R_i . k^R_j, scaled by 1/sqrt(d_h + d_h^R)
code_task: MLA.forward(x, mode='absorb'): w_uk (H, nope, d_c), w_uv (H, v, d_c) from wkv_b; einsum-based scores over c_kv (B,S,d_c) and k_pe (B,S,d_rope); decode_step(x_t, cache) reading only the latent cache.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(mla(x, mode='absorb'), mla(x, mode='naive'), atol=1e-10, rtol=1e-10) in float64, including a single-token decode against a 1000-token cache; negative control with RoPE on the content key fails to match.
gotchas: Applying kv_norm in one path and not the other, since the latent must be normalized before both absorption and decompression; reshaping wkv_b as (H, d_c, nope+v) instead of (H*(nope+v), d_c) scrambles heads silently; forgetting that the softmax scale still uses nope+rope dims even though the absorbed query has d_c dims.
interview_q: Why can't you absorb W^UK into the query when RoPE is applied to keys, and how does DeepSeek fix it? RoPE inserts a rotation that depends on the relative position between the matrices, so their product can't be precomputed; DeepSeek leaves the compressed path position-free and adds separate small RoPE query dims and one shared RoPE key per token.
explainer: Here is the score between a query and a cached latent. The key in the middle is the up projection times the latent.
Matrix multiplication is associative. So slide that up projection off the key and onto the query.
Now the query lives in latent space, and we dot it straight against the cache. No keys are ever rebuilt.
Values work the same way. Average the latents first, then apply the up projection once at the end.
Now add RoPE to the content key. A rotation appears between the two matrices, and it depends on position.
That rotation changes for every pair of tokens, so the product can't be computed ahead of time. Absorption breaks.
DeepSeek's fix: keep the compressed path free of position, and send position through a small separate channel.
Total score equals latent score plus RoPE score. Absorbed and naive outputs now match to ten decimal places.

hook: Mixtral has 47 billion parameters and uses about 13 billion per token. A tiny linear layer decides which 13.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Mixtral has 47 billion parameters and uses about 13 billion per token. A tiny linear layer decides which 13.

0:15 QUESTION — DeepSeek-V3 is 671B total with 37B active. Most frontier models are now mixture of experts. The core is a router and top-k gating, and the hard engineering is what happens when too many tokens pick the same expert. We build the layer and plot expert usage.

1:00 INTUITION — Replace one big MLP with eight smaller ones and a receptionist. Each token goes to the receptionist, who scores all experts and sends the token to its top two. Output is a weighted mix of those two. Capacity means each expert can only see so many tokens per batch. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Router logits g = x W_r, W_r in R^{d x E}. Mixtral top-2: select indices of the top k logits, weights = softmax over those k logits only. y = sum_{i in topk} w_i * Expert_i(x), each expert a SwiGLU MLP. Switch top-1: y = p_i(x) Expert_i(x) with p = softmax over all E. Capacity: C = ceil(capacity_factor * tokens * k / E). Tokens beyond C for an expert are dropped (they pass through the residual only). Active parameters: shared params + k * expert params. Mixtral: 8 experts, top-2, 46.7B total, 12.9B active. FLOPs per token scale with active, memory with total.

4:30 CODE — class MoE(nn.Module) with n_experts, top_k, dim, hidden; self.router = nn.Linear(dim, n_experts, bias=False); self.experts = nn.ModuleList of SwiGLU. forward(x (B,T,d)): flatten to (N,d), logits (N,E), topk_vals, topk_idx = logits.topk(k), weights = topk_vals.softmax(-1). Dispatch loop: for e in range(E): mask = (topk_idx == e), token_ids, slot = mask.nonzero(as_tuple=True), out.index_add_(0, token_ids, weights[token_ids, slot, None] * expert(x[token_ids])). Optional capacity: keep the first C token_ids per expert. Return out and router stats (counts per expert, mean prob per expert). Swap into your GPT's MLP and train on TinyStories for a few hundred steps on the Mac.

8:30 RECEIPT — Instantiate Hugging Face transformers' Mixtral sparse MoE block with a tiny config (hidden 64, intermediate 128, 8 experts, top-2), copy router and expert weights, and torch.testing.assert_close(my_moe(x)[0], hf_block(x)[0], atol=1e-5). Also a dense-equivalence check: with top_k = E and equal router weights, the output equals the mean of all experts.

10:30 MEASURE — Expert utilization histogram at step 0, 100, 500: fraction of tokens per expert per layer. Also tokens dropped vs capacity factor 1.0, 1.25, 2.0. Without balancing you will likely see a few experts take most tokens. That is next episode's problem.

11:45 TAKEAWAY — An MoE layer is a router, top-k selection, a weighted sum of a few expert MLPs, and a capacity limit. Interview line: MoE decouples parameters from FLOPs per token; compute scales with active experts while memory and communication scale with total experts.
12:30 NEXT — Next: MoE load balancing.
key_math: g = x W_r; I = topk(g, k); w = softmax(g_I); y = sum_{i in I} w_i E_i(x); C = ceil(cf * N * k / E); active params = shared + k * expert

receipt: Copy weights into transformers' Mixtral sparse MoE block (tiny config) and torch.testing.assert_close(my_moe(x)[0], hf_block(x)[0], atol=1e-5); top_k=E with uniform router equals mean of experts.
gotchas: Softmax over all experts then top-k without renormalizing, versus Mixtral's softmax over the selected logits (they differ unless you renormalize); a Python loop over tokens instead of over experts is thousands of times slower; index_add_ on fp16 accumulates poorly, accumulate in fp32.
interview_q: What is the difference between total and active parameters in an MoE, and what does each cost? Total parameters set memory footprint and, with expert parallelism, communication; active parameters (shared plus k experts) set FLOPs per token. Mixtral is 46.7B total but about 12.9B active, so it computes like a 13B model but needs memory for 47B.
explainer: Here is a transformer block with one big MLP. Every token pays for every parameter.
Split the MLP into eight smaller experts, and put a tiny router in front of them.
A single token arrives at the layer. The router, one small linear layer, gives it eight scores, one per expert.
Keep only the top two scores. Softmax just those two to get the mixing weights for this token.
The token runs through only those two experts. Their outputs are blended by the weights.
Across the batch, tokens fan out to different experts. Each expert processes its own little group.
Each expert has a capacity. Tokens that arrive after it is full are dropped and skip the layer.
Watch the bar chart. Without any balancing, a couple of experts end up doing most of the work.

The utilization plot shows the core problem of MoE: without balancing, a few experts take most tokens. Next I implement the fixes.

hook: Left alone, an MoE router collapses onto a few experts. DeepSeek-V3 fixes it without an auxiliary loss, using one bias per expert.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Left alone, an MoE router collapses onto a few experts. DeepSeek V3 fixes it without an auxiliary loss, using one bias per expert.

0:15 QUESTION — Collapse wastes parameters and, with expert parallelism, overloads some GPUs while others idle. Switch Transformers added an auxiliary loss. DeepSeek-V3 argued that loss hurts quality and replaced it with a bias nudged up or down each step. We build both and the collapse demo.

1:00 INTUITION — A rich-get-richer loop: an expert that gets more tokens trains more, gets better, gets picked more. The aux loss is a tax on popularity added to the objective. DeepSeek's bias is more like a traffic light at each expert: if it is overloaded, make it look slightly less attractive for routing only, without touching the gradient. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:00 MATH — Switch aux loss: L_aux = alpha * E * sum_i f_i * P_i, where f_i = fraction of tokens whose top choice is expert i, P_i = mean router probability for expert i over the batch, alpha = 0.01. At perfectly uniform routing f_i = P_i = 1/E, so L_aux = alpha * E * E * (1/E^2) = alpha. f is not differentiable; the gradient flows through P. Router z-loss (ST-MoE): mean (logsumexp(logits))^2, coefficient about 1e-3. DeepSeek-V3: affinity s_i = sigmoid(u^T e_i). Select top-K by s_i + b_i. Gate weight g_i = s_i / sum_{j in topK} s_j uses the raw s, not the bias. After each step: b_i <- b_i - gamma if expert i is overloaded, b_i + gamma if underloaded, gamma = 0.001 for most of training. Plus a tiny sequence-wise balance loss with alpha = 0.0001. Metric MaxVio = (max_i load_i - mean load) / mean load.

5:30 CODE — Three routers on your MoE: route_plain, route_aux (returns aux loss computed from counts and probs), route_bias with self.register_buffer('bias', torch.zeros(E)) updated under torch.no_grad() after optimizer.step(): load = counts; self.bias += gamma * torch.sign(load.float().mean() - load). Train the same small MoE GPT (8 experts, top-2) three times on TinyStories, same seed, log per-step MaxVio and validation loss. Optional fourth run with Switch top-1 to show collapse is faster with k=1.

8:30 RECEIPT — Analytic check: assert abs(switch_aux_loss(uniform_logits) - alpha) < 1e-6. Implementation check: compare your aux loss against Hugging Face transformers' Mixtral load_balancing_loss_func on the same router logits (note it computes the top-k version with an alpha of 1 by default, so match its convention). Behavior check: the bias run's MaxVio drops below the plain run's within a few hundred steps, as in DeepSeek's loss-free balancing results.

10:30 MEASURE — Three panels: MaxVio vs step for plain, aux, bias; validation loss vs step for the three; expert-load heatmap (layer x expert) at the end. Report the final val loss gap between aux and bias honestly, at this tiny scale it may be within noise, so run 3 seeds.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Aux loss balances by adding a gradient penalty; DeepSeek-V3 balances by adjusting a routing-only bias with no gradient interference. Interview line: the bias changes which experts are selected but not the gating weights, so balancing pressure never competes with the language modeling loss.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Sliding-window attention and attention sinks.
key_math: L_aux = alpha E sum_i f_i P_i (=alpha when uniform); z-loss = mean(logsumexp(logits)^2); DeepSeek-V3: topK by s_i + b_i, g_i = s_i / sum_{topK} s_j, b_i <- b_i + gamma sign(mean_load - load_i), gamma=0.001; MaxVio = (max load - mean load)/mean load
code_task: route_plain, route_aux (returns L_aux), route_bias (sigmoid affinities, bias buffer (E,), no-grad update after optimizer.step); training script for three 8-expert top-2 MoE GPTs on TinyStories logging MaxVio, val loss, per-layer expert counts.
receipt: abs(switch_aux_loss(uniform) - alpha) < 1e-6; aux loss matches transformers' Mixtral load_balancing_loss_func on identical logits after convention alignment; bias-routing MaxVio falls below plain-routing MaxVio across 3 seeds.
gotchas: Using the biased score s_i + b_i as the gate weight, which leaks the balancer into the forward pass; updating the bias inside autograd so it gets gradients or is touched by weight decay; computing f_i per micro-batch on tiny batches gives noisy loads, aggregate over the global batch.
interview_q: How does DeepSeek-V3 balance experts without an auxiliary loss? Each expert has a bias added to its affinity only for top-K selection; after each step the bias is decreased for overloaded experts and increased for underloaded ones by a fixed step, so load evens out while gate weights and gradients come from the unbiased scores.
explainer: Here is our router after a few hundred steps with no balancing. Two experts are taking almost every token.
It is a feedback loop. More tokens mean more gradient updates, a better expert, and even more tokens.
Switch Transformers adds a penalty to the loss: fraction of tokens times average router probability, summed over all experts.
At perfect balance that penalty equals alpha exactly. Any imbalance pushes it higher, and its gradient pushes back.
But that extra gradient competes with the language modeling loss, and DeepSeek argued it measurably costs model quality.
Their fix: one bias number per expert, added to the score only when choosing the top K.
After each step, overloaded experts get their bias lowered a notch, underloaded ones raised a notch.
The gate weights still use the clean scores. On the plot, load evens out and the loss curve is untouched.

hook: Delete the first four tokens from a model's cache and it starts speaking gibberish. Those tokens are attention sinks, and they hold everything up.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Delete the first four tokens from a model's cache and it starts speaking gibberish. Those tokens are attention sinks, and they hold everything up.

0:15 QUESTION — Mistral 7B used a 4096-token sliding window to bound memory. Gemma and gpt-oss mix sliding and global layers. But a naive rolling cache breaks models badly, and StreamingLLM found why. We build sliding-window attention, the rolling cache, and test sinks on a real model.

1:00 INTUITION — Sliding window says each token only looks at the last W tokens, like reading with a flashlight. Stack L layers and information still travels W times L back, like a bucket brigade. Attention sinks: softmax has to put its probability somewhere, and models learn to dump the excess on the first tokens. Evict them and the dump vanishes. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Sliding window mask: token i attends to j iff i - W < j <= i. Compute and cache per layer O(N W) and O(W) instead of O(N^2) and O(N). Receptive field after L layers is about L * W; Mistral 7B: 32 * 4096, about 131k tokens. Rolling buffer: position i stored at slot i mod W. Attention sink view: softmax_j(s_ij) = exp(s_ij) / sum_k exp(s_ik). If no token is relevant, probability still sums to 1, so the model parks it on always-visible early tokens. StreamingLLM keeps 4 sink tokens plus the recent window. Learned sink (gpt-oss style): add one extra logit per head to the denominator, softmax over [s_i1..s_iN, z_h], then drop the sink column.

5:00 CODE — def sliding_window_mask(N, W) -> bool (N,N). Use it two ways: SDPA with attn_mask, and torch.nn.attention.flex_attention with a mask_mod lambda b,h,q,kv: (q >= kv) & (q - kv < W) and create_block_mask, which skips fully masked blocks. class RollingKVCache(W, n_sink=0) with update(k, v, pos) that keeps the first n_sink entries pinned and writes others at n_sink + (pos - n_sink) mod (W - n_sink). Experiment: Qwen3-0.6B or TinyLlama generating perplexity over a long text (20k tokens, streamed), three caches: full (until OOM), window-only, sinks+window.

8:30 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(flex_attention(q,k,v, block_mask=swa_block_mask), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v, attn_mask=sliding_window_mask(N,W)), atol=1e-5) in float32. Learned sink: assert_close(sink_attention(q,k,v,z), reference that concatenates a column of z to the scores, softmaxes, and drops it). Published check: StreamingLLM reports window-only perplexity explodes once the initial tokens are evicted, while 4 sinks plus window stays flat. Reproduce the shape of that curve.

10:30 MEASURE — Perplexity vs tokens generated, three lines; window-only spikes at the first eviction. Memory vs N for full attention vs sliding window (flat). Attention heatmap from a middle layer showing heavy mass on token 0.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Sliding window bounds memory, stacking layers recovers range, and keeping a few sink tokens prevents collapse. Interview line: attention sinks exist because softmax must sum to one, so models park unused attention on early tokens, and evicting them shifts every attention distribution.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Beyond attention: SSMs and linear attention.
key_math: mask_ij = (j <= i) and (i - j < W); receptive field ~ L*W (Mistral 7B: 32*4096); slot = n_sink + (pos - n_sink) mod (W - n_sink); learned sink: p_ij = e^{s_ij} / (e^{z_h} + sum_k e^{s_ik})
code_task: sliding_window_mask(N, W); flex_attention mask_mod + create_block_mask version; RollingKVCache(W, n_sink) with update(k, v, pos); sink_attention(q, k, v, z (H,)); streaming perplexity experiment with full, window-only and sink+window caches.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(flex_attention(q,k,v,block_mask=swa_mask), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,attn_mask=sliding_window_mask(N,W)), atol=1e-5); sink_attention matches the concat-softmax-drop reference; window-only perplexity spikes at first eviction while 4-sink cache stays flat, matching StreamingLLM.
gotchas: Off-by-one in the window (i - j < W versus <= W) gives W+1 visible tokens and silent mismatches with the reference model; reapplying RoPE with cache-slot positions instead of original positions after the buffer wraps; SDPA with a dense bool mask still does O(N^2) work, only flex_attention block masks actually skip blocks.
interview_q: What are attention sinks and why does StreamingLLM keep them? Because softmax weights must sum to one, models learn to dump excess attention on the first few tokens; a rolling cache that evicts them changes every attention distribution and perplexity explodes, so StreamingLLM pins about four initial tokens alongside the recent window.
explainer: Here is a causal attention mask, the full lower triangle. Every token sees everything before it.
Sliding window keeps only a diagonal band. Each token sees just the last W tokens.
Stack layers and the band compounds. After L layers, information can travel L times W tokens back.
In memory, the KV cache becomes a ring buffer of W slots. Each new token overwrites the oldest slot.
Now look at a real attention map. Column zero is bright in almost every row. That is the sink.
Softmax must sum to one. When nothing is relevant, the model parks its attention on the first tokens.
Evict those first tokens and the parked attention spills onto everything else. On the plot, perplexity explodes immediately.
Pin four sink tokens next to the rolling window, and the curve stays flat for as long as we generate.

x_post: Sliding-window attention with a rolling KV cache sounds free. It isn't: evict the first tokens and perplexity explodes. Softmax must sum to 1, so models park attention on early tokens, the attention sinks. Keep 4 sinks + the window and it streams forever. Code + video:
linkedin: Implemented sliding-window attention with flex_attention block masks, a rolling KV cache, and attention sinks, then reproduced the StreamingLLM result on a small model: window-only caching makes perplexity explode at the first eviction, while pinning four initial tokens keeps it flat. Sinks exist because softmax has to sum to one.

hook: Remove the softmax from attention and a transformer becomes an RNN with a fixed-size memory. That is the idea behind linear attention and Mamba.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Remove the softmax from attention and a transformer becomes an RNN with a fixed size memory. That is the idea behind linear attention and Mamba.

0:15 QUESTION — Attention's cost grows with context, and so does its cache. Mamba, linear attention and their hybrids, like Jamba and Qwen3-Next's linear layers, promise constant memory per token. What do you give up? We build linear attention both ways and a tiny selective SSM.

1:00 INTUITION — Softmax attention keeps every past key and value and rereads all of them each step. Linear attention keeps one running d by d summary matrix and updates it per token. Mamba is the same shape of idea with a learned, input-dependent forgetting rate. Fixed memory means lossy memory. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Softmax attention: y_i = sum_j sim(q_i,k_j) v_j / sum_j sim(q_i,k_j), sim = exp(q.k). Replace sim with phi(q)^T phi(k), phi(x) = elu(x) + 1 (Katharopoulos et al. 2020). Causal: y_i = phi(q_i)^T S_i / phi(q_i)^T z_i with S_i = S_{i-1} + phi(k_i) v_i^T (d x d_v), z_i = z_{i-1} + phi(k_i). Per-token cost O(d d_v), independent of i. Parallel form for training: Y = ((phi(Q) phi(K)^T) masked lower-triangular) V, normalized. Selective SSM (Mamba): h_t = A_bar_t h_{t-1} + B_bar_t x_t, y_t = C_t h_t, with A_bar_t = exp(Delta_t A), B_bar_t approx Delta_t B_t, and Delta_t, B_t, C_t computed from x_t. That input dependence is the selection. Add a decay to linear attention, S_i = gamma S_{i-1} + k v^T, and the two families look alike.

5:30 CODE — def linear_attn_parallel(q,k,v) for (B,H,N,d): phi, scores = phi(q) @ phi(k).T, tril mask, normalize, @ v. def linear_attn_recurrent(q,k,v): loop over N keeping S (B,H,d,d) and z (B,H,d). def selective_scan(x, delta, A, B, C) with x (B,L,D), A (D,N), B and C (B,L,N): sequential loop keeping h (B,D,N). Tiny model: swap attention for linear attention in your GPT, train on TinyStories next to the softmax baseline for the same steps.

8:30 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(linear_attn_recurrent(q,k,v), linear_attn_parallel(q,k,v), atol=1e-5) in float32: same function, two algorithms. For the SSM, assert_close a chunked scan against your sequential reference. Then the published comparison: Mamba reports about 5x higher inference throughput than a same-size transformer; check your own decode memory: recurrent state bytes stay constant while the KV cache grows linearly.

10:30 MEASURE — Validation loss curves: softmax GPT vs linear-attention GPT at equal steps. Then a needle-in-a-haystack recall probe on a synthetic copy task: softmax solves it, linear attention degrades as length grows. Decode memory vs N, two lines.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Linear attention and SSMs compress history into a fixed-size state, which makes decode cheap and recall lossy. Interview line: without softmax, attention factorizes so the sum over keys can be carried as a running d by d state; Mamba adds input-dependent decay to choose what to keep.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Stability at scale: QK-norm, z-loss, Muon.
key_math: y_i = phi(q_i)^T S_i / phi(q_i)^T z_i; S_i = S_{i-1} + phi(k_i) v_i^T; z_i = z_{i-1} + phi(k_i); phi = elu + 1; Mamba: h_t = exp(Delta_t A) h_{t-1} + Delta_t B_t x_t, y_t = C_t h_t
code_task: linear_attn_parallel and linear_attn_recurrent for q,k,v (B,H,N,d) with state S (B,H,d,d), z (B,H,d); selective_scan(x (B,L,D), delta (B,L,D), A (D,N), B (B,L,N), C (B,L,N)) sequential and chunked; GPT variant with linear attention trained next to softmax baseline.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(linear_attn_recurrent(q,k,v), linear_attn_parallel(q,k,v), atol=1e-5); chunked selective scan equals sequential reference; recurrent decode state bytes constant in N versus linear KV-cache growth.
gotchas: Forgetting the normalizer z and getting outputs whose scale grows with position; phi that can go negative (plain identity) makes the denominator cross zero and nan; the parallel form materializes N x N and loses the whole point at long N, use the recurrent or chunked form for inference.
interview_q: Why can linear attention run as an RNN but softmax attention cannot? With a kernel feature map, sim(q,k) = phi(q)^T phi(k) factorizes, so sum_j phi(k_j) v_j^T can be accumulated into a fixed d x d state; the exponential in softmax does not factorize that way, so every past key must be kept.
explainer: Here is softmax attention at decode time. A new query looks back over every cached key, and the cache keeps growing.
Now drop the softmax and use a feature map instead. The score becomes a plain dot product of features.
That lets us reorder the sum. Add up key times value outer products first, into one square matrix.
That matrix is the whole memory. Each new token adds one outer product to it. Its size never changes.
Training uses the same math in parallel, a masked matrix product. Both forms give identical outputs.
Mamba keeps a state too, but each token decides how much of the old state to forget.
Fixed memory is cheap at decode. On the memory plot, the state line is flat while the KV cache climbs.
The cost is recall. Ask for a fact from far back, and the compressed state has partly forgotten it.

short: The re-bracketing step that turns attention into a d x d running state. Caption: 'Remove softmax and attention becomes an RNN.'
yt_title: Linear Attention and Mamba Explained: when attention becomes an RNN
x_post: Drop the softmax, use phi(q).phi(k), and attention becomes an RNN: S_i = S_{i-1} + phi(k_i) v_i^T, a fixed d x d memory. Mamba adds input-dependent forgetting. Built both forms, proved they match, then measured what fixed memory forgets. Code + video:
linkedin: Implemented linear attention in parallel and recurrent form, proved they're the same function, and built a small selective scan in the style of Mamba. Then I measured the tradeoff: constant decode memory, but worse long-range recall on a copy task than softmax attention. Fixed-size state is cheap and lossy.

hook: Big training runs do not die from bad ideas. They die from one attention logit growing until the loss spikes. Three tricks stop it.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Big training runs do not die from bad ideas. They die from one attention logit growing until the loss spikes. Three tricks stop it.

0:15 QUESTION — Qwen3, OLMo 2 and Gemma 3 use QK-norm. PaLM used z-loss. The NanoGPT speedrun and Kimi K2 use Muon. These are the stability and efficiency tricks every frontier pretraining team knows. We provoke a loss spike on purpose and ablate the fixes.

1:00 INTUITION — Attention logits are q dot k. If weights grow, logits grow, softmax saturates to one-hot, gradients become huge or vanish, and the loss jumps. QK-norm puts a governor on q and k. z-loss keeps the output softmax normalizer near one. Muon makes each weight update well-conditioned so no single direction runs away. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — QK-norm: q <- RMSNorm(q) * g_q, k <- RMSNorm(k) * g_k per head, so |q.k| is bounded by d times the gains. z-loss: L_z = 1e-4 * (log Z)^2, Z = sum_v exp(logit_v), pushes log Z toward 0 so logits do not drift (PaLM). Muon: for a 2D weight W with momentum buffer M = beta M + G, update O = NewtonSchulz5(M), an approximate orthogonalization U V^T of M = U S V^T. Iteration X <- a X + b (X X^T) X + c (X X^T)^2 X with (a,b,c) = (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315), 5 steps, X_0 = M / ||M||_F. Apply Muon to hidden 2D matrices, AdamW to embeddings, head and gains.

5:00 CODE — Add qk_norm flag to your attention (two nn.RMSNorm(head_dim)). Add z_loss term in the training loop: lse = logits.logsumexp(-1); loss = ce + 1e-4 * lse.pow(2).mean(). Write def newton_schulz5(G, steps=5) and class MyMuon(torch.optim.Optimizer). Spiky config: small GPT, lr 3x too high, no warmup, bf16. Runs: baseline, +QK-norm, +z-loss, +both, and Muon vs AdamW at tuned lr. Log max attention logit per layer and loss.

8:30 RECEIPT — Muon: for a random 256x128 matrix, singular values of newton_schulz5(G) all lie roughly in [0.65, 1.2] (it is a loose orthogonalization by design; a square random matrix has some near-zero singular values that 5 steps cannot lift, so use a rectangular one). Then compare your optimizer step to torch.optim.Muon with the same lr, momentum, nesterov and ns_coefficients, and adjust_lr_fn set to match your scaling: torch.testing.assert_close on parameters after one step. QK-norm receipt: max attention logit stays bounded in the +QK-norm run while it grows in baseline.

10:30 MEASURE — Loss curves for the four stability runs with spikes circled; max attention logit vs step per run. Muon vs AdamW: steps to reach a fixed val loss, compared with the speedrun's reported gains from Muon (as published in modded-nanogpt).

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Bound the logits with QK-norm, anchor the normalizer with z-loss, and condition updates with Muon. Interview line: loss spikes usually come from attention or output logit growth, so modern recipes normalize q and k, add a small z-loss, and sometimes orthogonalize updates.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Why distribute: the memory wall.
key_math: q <- RMSNorm(q) g_q, k <- RMSNorm(k) g_k; L_z = 1e-4 (log sum_v e^{z_v})^2; Muon: O = NS5(M), X <- aX + b(XX^T)X + c(XX^T)^2 X, (a,b,c)=(3.4445,-4.7750,2.0315), X_0 = M/||M||_F
code_task: qk_norm flag in attention (nn.RMSNorm(head_dim) on q and k); z-loss term; newton_schulz5(G (m,n), steps=5); MyMuon optimizer for 2D params with AdamW for the rest; ablation script logging loss and max attention logit per layer.
receipt: Singular values of newton_schulz5(randn(256,128)) in roughly [0.65, 1.2]; torch.testing.assert_close(params after MyMuon step, params after torch.optim.Muon step) with matched lr, momentum, nesterov, ns_coefficients, adjust_lr_fn; max attention logit bounded with QK-norm and growing without.
gotchas: Applying Muon to embeddings or the LM head, which the method excludes; running Newton-Schulz on a tall matrix without transposing to the wide orientation first so X X^T is the small side; comparing to torch.optim.Muon without matching its learning-rate adjustment, which scales updates by matrix shape.
interview_q: Your pretraining run has periodic loss spikes. What do you check and try? Log max attention and output logits per layer; if they grow, add QK-norm and a small z-loss, lower or warm up the learning rate, check for bad data batches, and consider gradient clipping or an optimizer like Muon that conditions updates.
explainer: Here is a loss curve from our spiky config. Smooth, then a sudden jump. Training never quite recovers.
Underneath, plot the largest attention logit in each layer. It climbs steadily right before the spike.
Big logits push softmax to one hot. Gradients through it explode or vanish. That is the spike.
QK norm normalizes every query and key per head. Now the dot product has a ceiling.
At the output, z loss gently pulls the log of the softmax normalizer toward zero, so logits cannot drift.
Muon looks at each weight update as a matrix and orthogonalizes it with five Newton Schulz steps.
Every singular value of the update ends up near one. No single direction gets a giant step.
Now rerun the same config with the fixes turned on. The max logit flattens out and the loss curve goes smooth.

yt_title: QK-Norm, z-loss and Muon: fixing loss spikes in LLM training
x_post: Loss spikes usually trace to one thing: attention logits growing until softmax saturates. QK-norm caps q.k, z-loss anchors log Z, Muon orthogonalizes updates via 5 Newton-Schulz steps. Provoked a spike, ablated all three, matched torch.optim.Muon. Code + video:
linkedin: Provoked loss spikes in a small GPT on purpose and ablated three stability tools: QK-norm, z-loss and the Muon optimizer, logging max attention logits per layer to show the cause. My Muon implementation matches torch.optim.Muon after one step. Monitoring logits is the cheapest early warning a training run has.
